items.text: Images of identity components
$f\colon G\to H$ a homomorphism, $f$ generalising (as in the lemma). Then $f(G^0)=H^0$.

Proof. The maps $\varphi_x\colon G\to H$ are translates of $f$, hence generalising; so a subset of $H$ is stable under $G^0$ iff it is stable under specialisation and generalisation. $f(G^0)$ is stable under $G^0$, hence under specialisation and generalisation; it contains $e$, hence the generic point of $H^0$, hence $H^0$.
In the lemma $f(X^0)$ is an irreducible component of $Y$: $f(X^0)$ is stable under $G^0$ ($X^0$ is), hence under specialisation and generalisation.
Factorisation of a homomorphism
$G\to H$ with $G$ of finite type, $K=\operatorname{Ker}$. Then $G/K$ exists (fpqc), is a group of finite type, and
G\to G/K\hookrightarrow H\qquad(\text{epimorphism then monomorphism})

A monomorphism of groups of finite type is a closed immersion (closed immersion at one point, then translate). So the image of a homomorphism of algebraic groups is closed; unlike Lie groups (dense windings on a torus).
Structure of group schemes over a field
"Unscrewing" a group in steps. First, separable, totally discontinuous groups ($G^0$ a point):
constant groups $\Gamma_k$; étale groups = ordinary groups $\Gamma$ with a continuous action of $\Pi=\operatorname{Gal}(\bar k/k)$ (stabilisers $\Pi_x$ open).
pro-étale groups (inverse limits of finite étale groups) = compact totally disconnected groups $K$ with a continuous action of $\Pi$ ($\Pi\times K\to K$).
In general: locally compact totally disconnected groups with a continuous $\Pi$-action (an open compact subgroup).
Second, radicial groups ($G_{\mathrm{red}}=e$): affine, inverse limits of radicial groups of finite type; reduced to groups finite and radicial over $k$.
Third, groups separable and connected.
Conjecture. A separable connected group $G$ over $k$ is an extension of a group $G_0$ of finite type by an affine group $R\subset G$,
1\to R\to G\to G_0\to1,\qquad G\to G_0\ \text{faithfully flat and quasi-compact}

$k$ perfect, Chevalley: a smooth connected algebraic group is an extension of an abelian variety (proper, smooth, connected) by an affine group; the affine kernel is the largest smooth connected affine subgroup, canonically determined.
So conjecturally: any connected separable group scheme is an extension of an abelian scheme by an affine group; the extension is unique.

Equivalent: $G=\varprojlim G_i$, a filtering projective system of smooth connected groups of finite type with affine transition morphisms; this requires a bound on the dimensions of the maximal abelian quotients of the $G_i$.
Three-step dévissage of any $G$

$G^0$ with the induced structure sheaf is a scheme (connected component of a quasi-compact quasi-separated scheme: inverse limit of its open and closed neighbourhoods, affine transitions). If $k$ is perfect, $G^0_{\mathrm{red}}$ is a subgroup:
G\ \supset\ G^0\ \supset\ G^0_{\mathrm{red}};\qquad G/G^0\ (\text{type 1}),\quad G^0/G^0_{\mathrm{red}}\ (\text{type 2, radicial}),\quad G^0_{\mathrm{red}}\ (\text{type 3, smooth connected})
Functorial in $G$.
Radicial groups

Characteristic $0$: radicial groups are trivial. Characteristic $p$: for $G$ finite radicial, the Frobenius $F\colon G\to G^{(p)}$ (base change along $x\mapsto x^p$). $G$ is of height one if $F$ is trivial.
\operatorname{Ker}F\subset\operatorname{Ker}F^2\subset\cdots,\qquad \operatorname{Ker}F^{n}/\operatorname{Ker}F^{n-1}\ \text{of height one};\quad\text{height }n:\ F^n\ \text{trivial}
Theorem. Finite radicial groups of height one over $k$ $\simeq$ restricted $p$-Lie algebras of finite dimension over $k$ (Lie algebra with a $p$-th power map).
Jacobson's formula: for $x,y$ in a non-commutative algebra of characteristic $p$, $(x+y)^p=x^p+y^p+$ (terms in brackets of $x,y$).

$G\mapsto\operatorname{Lie}(G)\subset$ hyperalgebra, with bracket $xy-yx$ and $p$-th power ($p$-th power of a derivation is a derivation); $\operatorname{Lie}(G)=\operatorname{Lie}(G_1)$ for $G_1=\operatorname{Ker}F$: it sees only the first-order infinitesimal neighbourhood of $e$.

Simple restricted $p$-Lie algebras over an algebraically closed field: the commutative ones ($\alpha_p$, $\mu_p$), and otherwise the classical ones, from the simple algebraic groups of the Cartan–Killing types, and those of Cartan type ($W,S,H,K$, e.g. the Witt algebra of dimension $p$), with further ones in characteristic $\le5$. (Information in SGA 3.)
Smooth connected groups of finite type
Extension of an abelian variety by an affine group: abelian varieties on one side; affine groups on the other.
